t: Longest Non-decreasing Subarray From Two Arrays — Paired DP
o: At each index we pick nums1[i] or nums2[i] into nums3, maximizing the longest non-decreasing run. Track two DP values per index: the longest valid run ending at i if we chose nums1[i] (call a) or nums2[i] (call b). Each extends from whichever previous choice is ≤ the current pick. Example 2: choosing 1,2,3,4 builds a run of 4. This is O(n) versus exponential choice enumeration.
k: Two DP states per index (ended on nums1[i] vs nums2[i]) suffice since only the last chosen value matters.

a.i: a_i = 1 + max(prev choices ≤ nums1[i]), b_i defined symmetrically; answer is the max over all states.
s: For each i, compute new a from previous a/b when the corresponding previous value ≤ nums1[i]; likewise new b.
Update the answer with both new values.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def maxNonDecreasingLength(self, nums1: List[int], nums2: List[int]) -> int:
        a = b = ans = 1
        for i in range(1, len(nums1)):
            na = 1 + max(a if nums1[i-1] <= nums1[i] else 0,
                         b if nums2[i-1] <= nums1[i] else 0)
            nb = 1 + max(a if nums1[i-1] <= nums2[i] else 0,
                         b if nums2[i-1] <= nums2[i] else 0)
            a, b = na, nb
            ans = max(ans, a, b)
        return ans

a.t: O(n) — single pass with constant work per index

w: This two-state DP pattern generalizes to k arrays. Pitfall: resetting to 1 correctly when neither previous value fits, and comparing against the right previous element for each state.
